title: Newton's Laws of Motion (Foundations of Dynamics)
notes: Newton's first law says a body stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed, unless a net external force acts on it. A frame in which this is true is an inertial frame.

The second law gives the size and direction of the effect. The net force equals the rate of change of momentum. When the mass is constant this is F_net = ma, and the acceleration points the same way as the net force.

The third law says forces come in pairs. If body A pushes body B, body B pushes body A with the same magnitude and the opposite direction. The two forces act on different bodies, so they do not cancel on one free-body diagram.
Mass measures inertia. For the same net force, a larger mass has a smaller acceleration. Weight is the gravitational force W = mg and is not the same quantity as mass.

A free-body diagram shows only the forces acting on the body you chose. Contact forces such as the normal force and friction are drawn at the surface. The weight is drawn at the centre of gravity, downward.
The normal force from a table and the weight of a book are not a third-law pair. The third-law partner of the book's weight is the gravitational pull of the book on the Earth.

**Newton’s three laws (classified)**

| Law | Statement | Everyday example |
|---|---|---|
| First (inertia) | Body keeps state unless net force acts | Passengers lurch when bus brakes |
| Second | F = ma; rate of change of momentum | Push a loaded trolley |
| Third | Equal and opposite reaction pairs | Walking pushes ground back |
| Frame note | First law defines inertial frames | Accelerating bus is non-inertial |

**Force pairs bookkeeping**

| Pair | Action | Reaction |
|---|---|---|
| Book–table | Weight of book on table | Normal force on book? No — contact pair |
| Book–Earth | Earth pulls book | Book pulls Earth |
| Walking | Foot pushes ground backward | Ground pushes foot forward |
| Rocket | Gas pushed down | Rocket pushed up |

**Newton's laws — classified by role**

| Law | Statement | Role |
|---|---|---|
| First | No net force, no change of motion | Defines inertia |
| Second | F = ma | Quantifies force |
| Third | Equal opposite pairs on different bodies | Explains recoil |

exercises.question: A 2.0 kg block on a smooth horizontal table is pulled horizontally by 10 N. Find the acceleration.
steps: The table is smooth, so the friction force is zero.
Vertically, the normal force balances the weight, so the vertical acceleration is zero.
The horizontal net force is 10 N.
The acceleration is horizontal, in the direction of the pull.
exercises.answer: 5.0 m/s^2 in the direction of the 10 N pull.

topicTitle: Newton's Laws of Motion (Foundations of Dynamics)

subtopics.name: First law — inertia
points: A body remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force
Defines force as the cause of change in motion
Inertia is the resistance to change in motion, measured by mass

subtopics.name: Second law — F = ma
points: Net force equals rate of change of momentum: F = dp/dt
For constant mass this reduces to F = ma
Force and acceleration are both vectors, in the same direction

subtopics.name: Third law — action-reaction
points: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
The pair acts on DIFFERENT bodies, which is why they do not cancel
Explains walking, rocket propulsion and recoil

subtopics.name: Free body diagrams
points: Draw every force acting ON the body, never forces it exerts
Choose axes along the likely acceleration
Resolve forces and apply F = ma along each axis

subtopics.name: Common force types
points: Weight mg downward, normal reaction perpendicular to the surface
Tension along the string, friction opposing relative motion
Spring force proportional to extension

subtopics.name: Inertial and non-inertial frames
points: Newton's laws hold only in inertial (non-accelerating) frames
In an accelerating frame a pseudo force -ma must be added
Centrifugal force is a pseudo force of this kind

subtopics.name: Limits of validity
points: Fails at speeds near c — special relativity is required
Fails at atomic scales — quantum mechanics is required
Within its domain it is exact, which is why engineering still uses it
